concepts.title: Enzyme Classes and Cofactor Helpers
concepts.definition: Every catalyst of the cell is a protein except the few catalytic RNAs called ribozymes; the I.U.B. files them into seven reaction classes from oxidoreductases to the newer translocases, and many need helpers - organic coenzymes built from vitamins, metal ions like zinc or magnesium, or a tightly bonded prosthetic group, the naked protein being the apoenzyme and the armed pair the holoenzyme.
concepts.key_idea: Reaction type fixes the class; vitamin-derived coenzymes and metal ions complete enzymes that cannot work alone.
question_patterns: list the seven classes of enzymes adopted by the I.U.B. with the reaction type each catalyses
differentiate apoenzyme holoenzyme and prosthetic group with one example
which vitamin precedes NAD and which precedes FAD - state the role of each coenzyme
name the metal ion cofactors of carbonic anhydrase and of DNA polymerase
what are isozymes - how many isozyme forms do hexokinase and lactate dehydrogenase show
why are ribozymes exceptions to the statement that all enzymes are proteins

solution_steps.explain: Electron transfer marks oxidoreductases, group transfer transferases, water-assisted cleavage hydrolases, and so on.
Loose organic helpers are coenzymes, loose metal ions are cofactors, covalently bound helpers are prosthetic groups.
Protein alone is apoenzyme; protein plus cofactor is the active holoenzyme.

worked_examples.q: Catalytic RNA molecules are called what?

concepts.title: Lock-Key and Induced Fit Models
concepts.definition: Fischer pictured the active site in 1894 as a rigid lock pre-cut for its substrate key, while Koshland argued in 1958 that the site flexes like a glove around the hand of the substrate, aligning catalytic groups only after binding; enzymes further show group, absolute, stereo and geometrical grades of specificity.
concepts.key_idea: Old model: rigid complementary pocket; modern model: the site reshapes around the substrate after contact.
question_patterns: compare the lock and key model with the induced fit model of substrate binding
who proposed the induced fit hypothesis and in which year
why is the induced fit comparison drawn with a hand and a glove
name the four kinds of enzyme specificity with one example each
why does D-amino acid oxidase attack only the D isomer - name the specificity type
what holds the substrate inside the active site - list the non-covalent forces

solution_steps.explain: Fischer 1894 rigid lock; Koshland 1958 flexible induced fit.
Pre-shaped pocket versus pocket that refolds on binding to align residues for catalysis.
Group specificity tolerates close relatives, absolute takes one substrate, stereo picks one isomer, geometry picks cis or trans.

worked_examples.q: Who proposed the induced fit model in 1958: Koshland or Fischer?

concepts.title: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
concepts.definition: Reaction speed bends to the environment: heating raises activity to an optimum near body temperature then denatures the protein, each enzyme peaks at its own pH from pepsin around 1-2 to alkaline phosphatase near 10-11, and rising substrate concentration lifts the rate only until every enzyme molecule is saturated.
concepts.key_idea: Bell curves for temperature and pH, and a saturation plateau for substrate, describe every catalytic optimum.
question_patterns: what happens to enzyme activity when temperature rises beyond the optimum - sketch the curve
does pepsin prefer an acidic or an alkaline optimum pH - what becomes of it in the duodenum
why do most enzymes of the human body work best near 37 degrees celsius
name the DNA polymerase of hot springs that stays active even at 100 degrees
why does extra substrate stop raising the rate after a point - describe the saturation state
compare the optimum pH of pepsin acid phosphatase and alkaline phosphatase

solution_steps.explain: Temperature, pH, substrate concentration or a modulator - each leaves a signature curve.
Bells for temperature and pH peak at the optimum; substrate concentration gives a rising curve that plateaus.
Taq polymerase and a few kinases survive 100 degrees; pepsin works at pH 1-2 while most enzymes prefer pH 6-8.

worked_examples.q: Pepsin peaks near what pH: 1-2 or 9-10?

concepts.title: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
concepts.definition: For a single-substrate reaction the initial speed follows a rectangular hyperbola: velocity equals Vmax multiplied by substrate level divided by the sum of Km and that level, so the rate is proportional to substrate when far below Km, plateaus at Vmax when far above, and hits exactly half of Vmax when the substrate level equals Km.
concepts.key_idea: Km is the substrate level that buys half the top speed; solve the hyperbola for any missing variable.
question_patterns: an enzyme shows Vmax of 60 umol per minute and Km of 3 mM - find the initial velocity at 2 mM substrate
define the Michaelis constant and state its meaning on the velocity curve
at what substrate concentration does a Michaelis-Menten enzyme run at half of its Vmax
derive the substrate level needed to reach a given fraction of Vmax from the Michaelis-Menten equation
what shape does the v0 against S curve take and why does it flatten at high substrate
who proposed the enzyme kinetics equation and in which year

solution_steps.explain: Substitute Vmax, Km and the substrate level into the Michaelis-Menten relation.
For a target velocity, first find how far Vmax still exceeds it.
Rearranging the equation gives S = Km times the target velocity divided by that headroom.

worked_examples.q: At substrate equal to Km, the reaction runs at what fraction of Vmax: half or double?

concepts.title: Enzyme Units, Katal and Specific Activity
concepts.definition: One enzyme unit converts a micromole of substrate per minute, the katal converts a full mole per second and equals six times ten to the seven units, and specific activity - units carried per milligram of protein - rises as an enzyme preparation gets purer.
concepts.key_idea: Scale between unit and katal by six times ten to the seven; divide activity by protein mass to measure purity.
question_patterns: how many international units equal one katal - show the conversion
convert 2.5 micromoles per minute of activity into enzyme units and into katals
a purification fraction holds 400 units of activity in 50 mg of protein - compute its specific activity
how long will 5 units of enzyme take to convert 75 micromoles of substrate
why did the I.U.B. discourage the enzyme unit in favour of the katal
what does specific activity reveal about an enzyme preparation during purification

solution_steps.explain: One katal packs six times ten to the seven enzyme units.
Units per milligram of protein is the purity index.

worked_examples.q: One enzyme unit converts how much substrate per minute: a micromole or a mole?

concepts.title: Competitive and Non-Competitive Inhibition
concepts.definition: Inhibitors slow catalysts either permanently, as penicillin wedging transpeptidase shut, or reversibly: look-alike inhibitors fight for the active site and only raise Km, distant-site inhibitors cripple the enzyme and only lower Vmax, and uncompetitive binders attack only the enzyme-substrate pair, moving both constants.
concepts.key_idea: Read the kinetic signature: Km up with Vmax untouched means competitive; Vmax down with Km untouched means non-competitive.
question_patterns: distinguish competitive non-competitive and uncompetitive inhibition on the basis of Km and Vmax changes
why cannot non-competitive inhibition be overcome by raising the substrate concentration
how does penicillin kill bacteria - name the enzyme it inhibits irreversibly
which anti-inflammatory drug blocks cyclooxygenase and what kind of inhibition is that
why does a competitive inhibitor leave Vmax unchanged at very high substrate levels
which complex does an uncompetitive inhibitor attack and which constants does it alter

solution_steps.explain: Same site as substrate means competitive; elsewhere on the enzyme means non-competitive; only on ES means uncompetitive.
Competitive: Km rises, Vmax unchanged. Non-competitive: Vmax falls, Km unchanged. Uncompetitive: both change.
Tight non-dissociating binding such as penicillin on transpeptidase or aspirin on cyclooxygenase is irreversible.

worked_examples.q: Competitive inhibition raises which constant: Km or Vmax?

concepts.title: Laws of Thermodynamics and Free Energy
concepts.definition: Energy bookkeeping follows two rules: internal energy shifts only by heat in minus work out, and the universe's disorder never falls; Gibbs merged them into the free-energy balance where the change equals the enthalpy change minus temperature times the entropy change, and a negative result marks a spontaneous process.
concepts.key_idea: Enzymes only cut the activation barrier - they never move the equilibrium or rewrite the free-energy total.
question_patterns: a reaction absorbs 40 kJ of heat while doing 15 kJ of work - find the change in internal energy
with enthalpy change of minus 40 kJ and entropy change of minus 0.1 kJ per kelvin at 298 K compute the free energy change
state the first law of thermodynamics and express it as an equation
what does the second law predict for the entropy of the universe in a spontaneous process
why do enzymes lower the activation energy but cannot alter the equilibrium of a reaction
define Gibbs free energy and explain the meaning of a negative value

solution_steps.explain: Internal energy change equals heat absorbed minus work done.
Gibbs: free-energy change equals enthalpy change minus temperature times entropy change.

worked_examples.q: A negative free-energy change marks a what process: spontaneous or impossible?

concepts.title: ATP the Universal Energy Currency
concepts.definition: Cells bank usable energy in adenosine triphosphate: breaking food or capturing light first charges ADP into ATP, and spending that charge - ATP to ADP plus inorganic phosphate - releases about 7.3 kcal per mole for biosynthesis, transport and muscle work, with some processes like the firefly flash stripping ATP all the way to AMP and pyrophosphate.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply moles of ATP spent by 7.3 kcal to price any energy-demanding cell job.
question_patterns: how much energy is liberated when 4 mmol of ATP are hydrolysed to ADP and inorganic phosphate
why is ATP called the universal currency of free energy
name the three phosphate-bearing forms of adenosine and how many phosphate groups each holds
which process in the firefly strips ATP to AMP and pyrophosphate
list four vital cell processes that draw on the free energy of ATP hydrolysis
differentiate exergonic from endergonic processes in the ATP cycle of the cell

solution_steps.explain: Each mole of ATP spent releases 7.3 kcal.
What remains of the liberated energy after a named requirement is the surplus.

worked_examples.q: Hydrolysing one mole of ATP releases about how many kcal: 7.3 or 73?

worked_examples.question_pattern: An enzyme has Vmax {vmax_val} umol per minute and Km {km_val} mM. Find the initial velocity at {s_val} mM substrate, and the substrate level needed to drive the reaction at {target_rate} umol per minute.

extracted_variables.vmax_val: maximum velocity in umol per minute
extracted_variables.target_rate: desired initial velocity in umol per minute

solution_template.explain: Insert the constants into the Michaelis-Menten relation.
How far the maximum still exceeds the wanted velocity.
S equals Km times the wanted velocity divided by the headroom.

worked_examples.source_ref: kebt104.txt section 4.2 (7.3 kcal per mol of ATP)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A muscle contraction hydrolyses {atp_moles} mmol of ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate. Find the energy released, and the surplus left after biosynthesis consumes {used_kcal} kcal of it.

solution_template.explain: 7.3 kcal are freed per mmol of ATP split.
Surplus energy is the remainder after the biosynthetic bill.
